strengths: First benchmark for evaluating LLM reasoning in computer architecture, filling a clear gap in LLM evaluation
Rigorous methodology: three-pronged data collection approach (synthetic, crowdsourced, academic exams) with expert validation; all 2,671 QAs reviewed by architecture-trained doctoral students
Thorough LLM-as-a-Judge validation with 85.35% agreement to human experts (comparable to 90.7% human-human agreement across 100 QAs)
Comprehensive evaluation framework with four complementary skills (Recall, Analyze, Design, Implement) providing fine-grained analysis beyond aggregate scores
Detailed failure mode analysis with concrete examples of model weaknesses (architectural semantics of code, unconventional assumptions, system state tracking, modality sensitivity)
Multimodal assessment (548 image+text questions) addresses importance of diagrams in architecture understanding
Large community effort (140+ contributors from 40 institutions) demonstrates meaningful investment
Full reproducibility: all evaluation prompts, methodology, and ethical disclosures provided in appendix
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: construction approach (synthetic generation, crowdsourcing, exam parsing, LLM-as-a-Judge) follows established patterns from MMLU-Pro and GPQA rather than introducing new techniques
Severe benchmark imbalance: only ~100 Design and ~77 Implement questions (3.8% and 2.9%) vs. 1,564 Recall questions (58.5%), limiting conclusions about higher-order reasoning despite claims
No ablation study comparing synthetic vs. crowdsourced vs. exam-derived questions despite 58% synthetic data; potential distribution shifts and quality differences unexamined

LLM-as-Judge limited to one model (Claude-3.7) for main results despite finding slightly different agreement with Gemini; no analysis of systematic biases or whether judge model's biases affect conclusions
Shallow root cause analysis: paper identifies what models fail on but provides limited investigation into why; failure modes illustrated with examples but lack quantitative prevalence analysis
No consideration of data contamination: academic exams and crowdsourced content may appear in training data; no attempt to assess or mitigate potential data leakage
Incomplete skill classification methodology: skills assigned via LLM without inter-rater agreement statistics or human validation, creating risk of mislabeled questions affecting conclusions
Missing investigation of model-skill-topic interactions: large performance variance (e.g., Design scores 18-87%) mentioned but not explained; unclear why GPT-5 excels at Design while others struggle
Limited practical guidance: unclear how practitioners should use benchmark results to improve LLMs; no discussion of training approaches or applications to agent design

strengths: Rigorous benchmark construction combining synthetic generation, crowdsourcing, and academic exams with expert validation
Well-motivated skills framework (Recall-Analyze-Design-Implement) grounded in architectural practice
Comprehensive empirical evaluation of 26 models across multiple skill categories and topics
Solid LLM-as-a-judge validation study comparing to human experts (85.35% agreement vs 90.7% human-human)
Extensive failure mode analysis with concrete examples of model limitations across four categories
Large community contribution (140+ contributors from 40 institutions)
Multimodal content with 548 questions including diagrams and visual reasoning tasks
weaknesses: Limited novelty for ICML: core finding (models struggle with reasoning vs recall) is unsurprising and lacks actionable insights into why or how to improve
Severe benchmark imbalance: 1,564 Recall vs 112 higher-order questions (Design+Implement), limiting utility for evaluating reasoning
Incomplete evaluation protocol: zero-shot only with no few-shot, chain-of-thought, or other prompting strategies that substantially improve LLM performance
Critical reproducibility gaps: dataset not committed to release; expert validation performed on only 8.9% of FRQs (100/1,124)
LLM-as-a-judge methodology concerns: 85.35% agreement below human baseline (90.7%), only single judge model tested, PARTIALLY-CORRECT downgraded obscures performance nuance
Missing critical analyses: no data contamination discussion, no question difficulty normalization, no model architecture analysis, no skill progression investigation
Vague expert validation details: no inter-rater reliability metrics, acceptance rates, or disagreement resolution procedures for crowdsourced questions

Methodological concern: synthetic questions described as naturally involving little reasoning contradicts goal of creating reasoning benchmark; LLM generation + LLM filtering may introduce systematic biases
Presentation issues: 61-page paper lacks focused narrative; main findings presented without urgency; no formal limitations section
Question quality comparison missing: no analysis of difficulty/quality differences between synthetic, crowdsourced, and exam-sourced questions

strengths: Addresses a clear and important gap: first comprehensive benchmark for LLM reasoning in computer architecture, a domain absent from existing evaluations
Rigorous three-pronged curation methodology combining synthetic data generation, academic exams, and expert crowdsourcing with multiple validation stages
Well-defined and intuitive skills framework (Recall, Analyze, Design, Implement) that systematically reveals significant performance gaps (32-39% drops from recall to higher-order skills)
Comprehensive validation: expert review at multiple stages, LLM-as-a-Judge agreement (85.35%) validated against human experts (90.7% human-human agreement), showing credible scalability

Detailed and actionable failure mode analysis with multiple concrete examples: architecture-semantics of code, unconventional assumptions, system state tracking, domain expertise heterogeneity, and modality sensitivity
Strong community engagement with 140+ contributors from 40 institutions, providing evidence of real stakeholder investment
Excellent presentation: clear writing, well-organized structure, comprehensive appendices with all prompts (D.1-D.10), and extensive documentation supporting reproducibility
Multimodal and mixed-format assessment: 1,547 MCQs and 1,124 free-response questions covering both text and diagrams, providing comprehensive skill evaluation
Thorough characterization of benchmark: 13 architecture topics, clear distribution, detailed skill coverage analysis, and relationship to existing benchmarks clearly positioned
weaknesses: LLM-as-a-Judge shows 5.4% gap from human-human agreement (85.35% vs 90.7%); limited analysis of which question types trigger disagreements; only 100 QAs sampled (3.7% of dataset) for validation is relatively small

Limited methodological novelty: curation techniques (synthetic generation, exam parsing, crowdsourcing) use established approaches; skills framework adapts existing educational taxonomy rather than introducing new concepts
No explicit statement of benchmark release plan, timeline, or licensing terms—reproducibility claims would be strengthened by concrete data availability details

Insufficient analysis of potential biases: no training data contamination risk assessment for frontier models; synthetic data generation uses LLM filtering before expert review (potential for bias propagation); expert panel composition not fully described

Limited actionable improvement guidance: identifies failure modes clearly but provides minimal concrete strategies for model improvement; no discussion of whether gaps require architecture-specific training, better prompting, or fundamental capability improvements

Experimental design limitations: zero-shot evaluation only (no few-shot or fine-tuning analysis); only 3 samples per question for stochastic evaluation; no confidence intervals or error bars on metrics
Multimodal performance gap (6% text-to-image drop) noted but insufficiently analyzed; which diagram types cause most failures is unclear

Small sample for human validation: 11 experts across 908 responses; inter-rater variance patterns and disagreement sources not analyzed; majority voting for 3 experts could hide meaningful disagreement

Benchmark-specific concerns: some architecture subfields potentially underrepresented (e.g., specialized accelerators, emerging architectures); skill framework may not be exhaustive; no difficulty distributions reported across domains

strengths: First dedicated benchmark for LLM reasoning in computer architecture, addressing a clear gap in evaluation methodology
Rigorous three-pronged benchmark construction (synthetic, academic exams, crowdsourced) with expert validation of all 2,671 QAs
Well-motivated four-skill framework (Recall, Analyze, Design, Implement) grounded in educational standards, enabling fine-grained capability assessment
Principled LLM-as-a-Judge validation: 85.48% agreement with humans comparable to 90.75% human-human agreement; analysis of self-judgment bias and alternative judges
Comprehensive evaluation of 10 frontier + 20 additional models with clear skill-wise performance breakdowns and detailed failure mode analysis
Concrete evidence of utility: fine-tuned models achieve 40% more viable designs and 1.99× area efficiency gains; strong correlation (r=0.726) with real design quality
Insightful analysis of four model failure modes (code semantics, architectural assumptions, state modeling, multimodal sensitivity) with concrete examples
Excellent reproducibility: all prompts provided, public leaderboard with hidden test set, detailed construction methodology, extensive supplementary materials
weaknesses: Severe imbalance in skill distribution (59% Recall, 36% Analyze, 1.6% Design, 3.7% Implement) undermines core motivation to evaluate higher-order reasoning; only 140 Design+Implement questions limits statistical reliability

Limited methodological novelty: four-skill taxonomy is standard educational framework; benchmark construction follows established patterns (synthetic + expert + crowdsourced); LLM-as-judge evaluation is well-established
Case studies limited in scope: only 45 filtered questions, only 2 open-source models, correlation shown but causation unclear, generalization to other tasks undemonstrated
Restricted evaluation protocol: zero-shot only with no systematic exploration of few-shot, chain-of-thought, or prompt sensitivity; no justification for 3-generation setting
Significant gap between QA format and real architectural practice (tool use, simulation, iteration, agent behavior); authors acknowledge but don't deeply explore implications
Incomplete statistical analysis: no confidence intervals, significance tests, or error bars; no expert inter-rater agreement analysis; multimodal gap (5%) mentioned but not investigated
LLM judge validation leaves 14.52% unexplained disagreement; no breakdown of which question types judges fail; no analysis of judge disagreements on Design/Implement questions
Presentation: 72-page document with extensive appendices; key results sometimes relegated to appendix; Figure 1 difficult to interpret; limited guidance on benchmark versioning and updates

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap in LLM evaluation for computer architecture, a domain absent from current benchmarks
Rigorous three-pronged benchmark construction combining synthetic generation, academic exams, and expert crowdsourcing with two-stage validation
Thorough LLM-as-a-judge validation achieving 85.48% human expert agreement (vs. 90.75% human-human) with transparent methodology and alternative judge comparison
Well-grounded skills framework (Recall-Analyze-Design-Implement) adapted from established educational taxonomies, enabling fine-grained capability analysis
Concrete knowledge transfer demonstration showing 1.99× area improvements and 40% more viable solutions on memory design tasks using proper simulation tools
Detailed identification of four failure modes (code semantics, unconventional assumptions, state modeling, domain expertise) with concrete examples
Multimodal representation with 548 image+text questions important for architectural reasoning evaluation
Evaluation of 10 frontier + 20 additional models (30 total) providing comprehensive coverage and detailed per-topic performance analysis
Honest acknowledgment of limitations (synthetic data reliance, design/implement underrepresentation) and transparent benchmark construction details
Public benchmark release with extensible crowdsourcing infrastructure enabling community contribution and growth
weaknesses: Over 58% of benchmark (1,547/2,671) is synthetically generated; despite two-stage filtering, quality assurance and potential systematic biases insufficiently addressed
Severely unbalanced skill distribution: Recall (59%), Analyze (36%), Design (1.6%), Implement (3.7%); only 140 design/implement QAs cannot reliably assess claimed higher-order reasoning capabilities
Empirical findings are modest and expected: LLMs struggle with architecture reasoning (34-73% on reasoning QAs), confirming general reasoning limitations without novel insights
Zero-shot evaluation only; no exploration of few-shot, chain-of-thought, or prompt engineering effects despite their known importance in modern LLM research
Missing statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, no justification for 3-sample choice, no significance testing between model comparisons, no random baselines

Knowledge transfer case studies are narrow: only 45 memory-focused FRQs used for fine-tuning; generalization to processor design or interconnect networks unclear; no ablation studies on which features drive improvements
Insufficient analysis of 5% multimodal performance gap; only 2 failure examples for images; unclear if architecture-specific or general vision-language limitation
LLM-as-judge limitations under-discussed: 14.52% human disagreement is non-trivial; self-judgment bias shows Gemini ~29% false positive rate; no per-question analysis of disagreement patterns
Reproducibility gaps: exact temperature/sampling parameters not specified, image encoding method unclear, API version details missing, prompts lack some specifics
Failure mode analysis is superficial: four modes identified but insufficient depth (e.g., are code semantics failures architecture-specific?); no frequency analysis or systematic categorization
Limited novelty: benchmark application is novel but construction approach is standard; skills framework adapts existing taxonomies; LLM-as-judge validation is rigorous but methodologically standard
Design choices lack justification: why mirror natural frequency in skill distribution rather than balance for evaluation purposes? Why 58% synthetic when quality alternatives exist?
No analysis of synthetic vs. crowdsourced QA quality differences, no memorization vs. reasoning decomposition, no specialized baseline comparisons
Presentation issues: 72-page appendix suggests scope creep; key results (alternative judges, per-topic analysis) relegated to appendix; dense main narrative
Leaderboard infrastructure mentioned (private hidden test, gated access) but enforcement and effectiveness of contamination prevention not demonstrated

strengths: Fills genuine gap: First comprehensive LLM benchmark for computer architecture reasoning—a clear and important omission in current evaluation landscape
Well-designed skills framework grounded in educational theory (ABET, ACM) that aligns with how architects actually practice systems design
Rigorous benchmark construction with multi-pronged approach (synthetic generation, academic exams, crowdsourcing) reducing single-source bias and including 2,671 expert-validated QA pairs
Comprehensive model evaluation with fine-grained analysis: 10+ frontier models across 4 skills, MCQ+FRQ formats, multimodal assessment, and clear failure mode identification
Rigorous LLM-as-judge validation (85.48% agreement with human experts, comparable to 90.75% human-human agreement) with cross-model agreement analysis strengthening confidence

Practical knowledge transfer demonstration: Memory hierarchy case study shows 1.99× area efficiency and 40% more viable solutions; DRAM controller case study shows significant correlation (r=0.726, p=0.007)
Exceptional reproducibility with comprehensive prompt appendices (D.1-D.12), public benchmark/leaderboard commitment, detailed methodology, and thoughtful ethics statement
Clear presentation with effective figures, logical flow, and appropriate supplementary material
Honest limitations discussion acknowledging design/implementation underrepresentation, multimodal gaps, and zero-shot scope
weaknesses: Advanced reasoning skills severely underrepresented: Only 5.2% Design/Implementation questions (140 of 2,671) despite emphasis on 'higher-order thinking'; 59% Recall questions limits ability to assess reasoning capabilities

No ablation on synthetic vs. crowdsourced data quality: 58% synthetic, 42% crowdsourced without analysis of whether synthetic questions from manuals achieve comparable difficulty/sophistication to crowdsourced submissions

Limited prompting strategy investigation: All evaluation zero-shot; no few-shot, chain-of-thought, or architecture-specific prompting explored despite emphasizing reasoning—results could shift substantially

Modest knowledge transfer case studies: Fine-tuning on only 45 filtered questions (676 total samples across 3 epochs); two models only; second case study shows correlation on 3 models without causal claims
Multimodal performance gap under-explored: 5% degradation on images (Table 7) is non-trivial for domain fundamentally reliant on visual reasoning, but limited analysis (Appendix C.5 only)
Missing human performance baselines: Cannot calibrate difficulty without student/architect/expert data; standard practice for reasoning benchmarks
Potential data leakage concerns: Academic exams and technical manuals likely in training data; no explicit decontamination methodology discussed
Future saturation risk: GPT-5.2 already at 73.2% on QUARCH-REASONING; extensibility discussion (Section 2.5) vague about executable artifacts roadmap
Model naming clarity unclear: Names like 'GPT-5.2,' 'Gemini-3-Pro' appear hypothetical; if actual, temporal framing needs clarification affecting reproducibility claims
Limited analysis of model-specific patterns: Spider plots show substantial topic variation but limited investigation of why different models excel in different domains
No per-question difficulty ratings or progression analysis—cannot assess calibration or identify instruction-focused clusters
Limited cross-domain transfer validation: Knowledge transfer shown only for memory subsystems; generalization to processor design, interconnects, etc. unexplored
